objective.statement: Name and write diatonic and chromatic intervals between any two notes.
successCriteria: I count the number in letter names and the quality from the semitones.
I know a chromatic interval is one whose notes are in no one major or minor scale.
I never name an interval from the sound alone.

explanation.text: A diatonic interval joins two notes that belong to the same major or minor scale; every interval you have met so far was diatonic. A chromatic interval joins two notes that no single scale contains: A♭ and F♯, for example. Most chromatic intervals can be named in the usual way: count the letters for the number, then find the quality.

music.textAlternative: Two semibreves: A flat then F sharp above it.

explanation.caption: A♭ up to F♯: six letters, so a 6th. A♭ to F is a major 6th; F♯ is a semitone larger: an augmented 6th.

explanation.text: Use the major scale of the lower note to find the quality. A♭ to F would be a major 6th. When the upper note is raised a semitone, major becomes augmented; when a minor interval is made a semitone smaller it becomes diminished (C♯ to A♭ is a diminished 6th, because C♯ to A♭ is a semitone smaller than the minor 6th C♯ to A).

Two intervals can sound the same and have different names. C up to A♯ is an augmented 6th, and C up to B♭ is a minor 7th, yet the two upper notes are the same key on the piano. The letter names decide the number, so never name an interval by its sound alone. Intervals that cannot be named with major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished (such as a doubly augmented 4th) are not asked. The octave can be altered too: from a note up to the same letter name in the next octave is a perfect 8th; C up to C♯ in the next octave is an augmented 8th (an octave plus a semitone), and C up to C♭ in the next octave is a diminished 8th (an octave less a semitone).
Number: count both letters. Quality: compare with the major scale of the lower note, or count semitones. The letter names, not the sound, fix the name.

steps: Count the letters: C D E F G A is six, so a 6th.
C♯ up to A♯ would be a major 6th (like C up to A); C♯ up to A natural is a minor 6th.
A♭ is a semitone smaller still: a diminished 6th.
demonstration.textAlternative: C sharp up to A flat: a diminished 6th.

guided.prompt: C up to A♯ is an augmented 6th. The upper note is now lowered by a semitone, to A. What is the interval now? Chromatic semitone: the letter name stays the same, so the number does not change.

d6.reason: The number stays 6. Raising the upper note makes the interval larger and lowering it makes it smaller: move one step along diminished – minor – major – augmented (perfect intervals sit between diminished and augmented).

m6.reason: The number stays 6. Raising the upper note makes the interval larger and lowering it makes it smaller: move one step along diminished – minor – major – augmented (perfect intervals sit between diminished and augmented).

A6.reason: The number stays 6. Raising the upper note makes the interval larger and lowering it makes it smaller: move one step along diminished – minor – major – augmented (perfect intervals sit between diminished and augmented).

hints: Larger by a semitone: minor to major, major or perfect to augmented.
Larger by a semitone: minor to major, major or perfect to augmented. Smaller: major to minor, minor or perfect to diminished.

feedback.correct: Yes: the number stays; the quality changes.

mistakes.counted-one-end-only: Count both the lower and the upper note.
mistakes.quality-from-wrong-key: Compare the upper note with the major scale of the LOWER note.
mistakes.compound-arithmetic: An octave plus a 5th is a 12th, not a 13th: the shared note is counted only once.
mistakes.enharmonic-spelling: The letter names decide the number, even when two spellings sound alike.
mistakes.augmented-diminished-swap: Larger by a semitone: diminished, minor, major, augmented.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Count the letter names first, then compare with the major scale on the lower note.

First Steps Grade 5 section 6 (pp. 112-113, read in the PDF): diatonic and chromatic intervals; chromatic intervals named like diatonic ones; intervals that cannot be so named are not asked (so no doubly augmented or diminished).
